prompt.context: Your client is Rubicon Co, a low-cost airline operating in the US. A couple of years ago, Rubicon Co completed the acquisition of Scarlet Air, an airline based primarily on the West Coast. The post-acquisition profits do not meet the executive committee's expectations, and the CEO of Rubicon Co has brought you in to understand the causes and improve profitability.
prompt.question: The CEO wants to increase profit by $100M. What are the causes of the profitability shortfall, and how would you improve profitability?

clarifying_info.q: What is the CEO's specific profit improvement target?
Does Rubicon Co operate multiple aircraft types?
clarifying_info.a: Assume a single aircraft type across the fleet with similar seat layouts.

clarifying_info.q: Is Rubicon Co considering premium cabin or business class?
clarifying_info.a: Rubicon Co is an all-economy airline and is not looking to change the business model.

clarifying_info.q: Is international expansion on the table?
clarifying_info.a: No, Rubicon Co is not looking to expand operations internationally at this point.

clarifying_info.q: How has the industry performed since the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: The industry has remained relatively stable, with single-digit profit percentage growth year over year.

clarifying_info.q: How did Rubicon Co and Scarlet Air compare to industry peers before the acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Pre-merger, both Rubicon Co and Scarlet Air met industry averages on financials.

exhibits.title: Pre and Post Acquisition Financials
exhibits.shows: A table comparing financial line items (Revenue from Tickets, Revenue from Non-Tickets, and cost line items: Operations/Variable, Marketing, IT, HR, PPE/Airport Slots & Offices) across three columns: Rubicon Co (Pre), Scarlet Air (Pre), and Rubicon Co (Post). All figures are in millions of dollars.

exhibits.title: Northwest Region Route Comparison
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing Revenue Per Seat and Cost Per Seat across three routes (Seattle-Denver, Portland-Seattle, Denver-Portland) for Rubicon Co and four competitors (Southeast Airlines, United, Gamma, US Fleet Co). A footnote states Rubicon Co flies approximately 500,000 passengers per route per year.

data.note: Rubicon Co flies ~500k passengers per route per year

framework: Revenue synergies: assess ticket revenue (price x volume) and non-ticket fees post-merger vs. combined pre-merger baseline
Cost synergies: compare each cost line item post-merger vs. the sum of pre-merger individual figures; identify where savings were not captured
Route-level profitability: analyze whether individual routes are profitable; flag loss-making routes
Competitive benchmarking: compare Rubicon Co's unit economics to competitors on key routes
Recommendations and risks: prioritize actions to close the $100M gap and identify associated risks

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What do you notice about the post-acquisition financials? Are there areas of opportunity to positively impact profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute totals and compare post-merger actuals to the sum of pre-merger figures. Revenue is fully combined (no loss). Variable/Operations costs are also essentially the sum (no cost savings yet). Fixed costs: HR and PPE show real synergies (savings already captured), but Marketing and IT remain at roughly the full combined total — those are the two cost-cutting opportunities. Strong candidates recognize that HR and PPE each achieved ~25% net savings and apply that same 25% benchmark to Marketing and IT.

math.setup: Compare post-merger cost line items to combined pre-merger totals. For Marketing: pre combined = 50+40=90; post = 90 (no savings yet). For IT: pre combined = 75+70=145; post = 145 (no savings yet). HR: pre combined = 20+14=34; post = 25.5 (savings of 8.5, ~25%). PPE: pre combined = 115+90=205; post = 153.75 (savings of 51.25, ~25%). Apply 25% savings benchmark to Marketing and IT.
steps: Total potential savings from Marketing + IT: 22.5 + 36.25 = 58.75
Post-merger profit (actual): Total Revenue = 1439+461=1900; Total Cost = 1255+90+145+25.5+153.75=1669.25; Profit = 1900-1669.25=230.75; Margin = 12.14%
Post-merger profit with synergy gains: Total Cost = 1669.25-58.75=1610; Profit = 1900-1610=289.50; Margin = 15.24%
Gap vs. $100M target: 289.50-230.75=58.75M improvement, leaving ~41.25M still to find
math.answer: Applying the same ~25% synergy rate to Marketing and IT yields approximately $58.75M in additional cost savings, getting about halfway to the $100M target.

questions.prompt: Brainstorming: Now that we have identified potential cost reductions in Marketing and IT, what are some specific ways these costs could be reduced?
questions.guidance: Candidate should suggest 2-3 ideas per bucket. Marketing: reduce headcount, leverage digital solutions to streamline campaigns, outsource specific functions. IT: reduce headcount, outsource specific functions, merge disparate legacy systems. Strong candidates also identify risks (morale impact from layoffs) and note that roughly half the $100M target is covered, prompting a search for additional profit sources.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 2. One of our analysts flagged the Pacific Northwest as an area of concern. What are your initial thoughts on these routes?
questions.guidance: Candidate should immediately identify that Portland-Seattle and Denver-Portland are loss-making (cost per seat exceeds revenue per seat) while Seattle-Denver is profitable. Strong candidates calculate total annual profit/loss per route using 500k passengers and then estimate the profit potential if Rubicon Co matches competitors' lower cost structure.

math.setup: For each route: Profit (Loss) Per Seat = Revenue Per Seat - Cost Per Seat. Total Net Profit (Loss) = Profit Per Seat x 500,000 passengers. Profit Potential = gap between Rubicon Co cost and best competitor cost x 500,000.
steps: Total current net across three routes: 45.5M-2M-10.5M=33M
Competitor cost benchmark (lowest) Seattle-Denver: 175; Portland-Seattle: 169; Denver-Portland: 160

Profit potential if matching competitor costs — Seattle-Denver: (215-175)*500k=20M additional; Portland-Seattle: (203-169)*500k=17M additional (converts loss to profit of 30*500k=15M); Denver-Portland: (210-160)*500k=25M additional (converts loss to profit of 29*500k=14.5M)
Total profit potential at competitor cost structure: 65.5M across three routes (vs. current 33M net), net improvement of ~62M
Combined with Marketing+IT synergies: 58.75M+62M=~120.75M, exceeding the $100M target
math.answer: The three Pacific NW routes together currently yield ~$33M net profit. If Rubicon Co matches competitors' cost structure, the routes could yield ~$65.5M, an improvement of ~$62M. Combined with the ~$58.75M from Marketing/IT synergies, total improvement reaches ~$120M, exceeding the $100M target.

questions.prompt: Brainstorming: Some within the company are thinking of cutting the loss-making routes completely. What concerns do you have with this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should think in both quantitative and qualitative buckets. Quantitative: cutting routes eliminates associated ancillary revenue (inflight purchases, fees, freight/cargo). Qualitative: knockback/network effect — passengers on these routes may connect to other profitable flights, so cutting them could reduce demand on profitable routes; political issues with city leadership; contractual airport obligations that may not allow easy exit. Strong candidates also suggest monitoring demand trends before making route decisions.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some specific ways Marketing and IT costs could be reduced? And separately, what concerns do you have about cutting loss-making Pacific NW routes?

categories.name: Marketing cost reduction
ideas: Leverage digital and programmatic solutions to streamline campaigns
Outsource specific marketing functions (e.g., creative, media buying)
Consolidate brand under a single Rubicon Co identity, eliminating Scarlet Air marketing spend

categories.name: IT cost reduction
ideas: Reduce headcount by eliminating duplicate IT roles
Merge disparate IT systems onto a single platform to reduce licensing and maintenance costs

categories.name: Concerns about cutting loss-making routes (quantitative)
ideas: Loss of ancillary fee revenue (baggage, change fees, inflight wifi/food)
Loss of freight and cargo revenue on those routes
Fixed costs may not be fully eliminated (gate leases, contractual obligations)

categories.name: Concerns about cutting loss-making routes (qualitative)
ideas: Knockback/network effect: passengers using these routes may connect to profitable flights, reducing load factors elsewhere
Political backlash from city and regional leadership
Airport contractual obligations that prevent easy route exit
Demand may improve seasonally or structurally — premature to cut
Brand/reputation impact in the Pacific Northwest market

recommendation: To achieve the $100M profitability improvement, Rubicon Co should apply the same ~25% synergy rate already achieved in HR and PPE to its Marketing and IT functions (~$58.75M savings), and work to match competitors' cost structure on its Pacific NW routes, particularly the loss-making Portland-Seattle and Denver-Portland routes (~$62M improvement potential), together exceeding the $100M target.
risks: Headcount reductions in Marketing and IT may depress employee morale and trigger attrition in other departments
Changes in demand on Pacific NW routes could affect pricing and profitability assumptions
Cutting loss-making routes could hurt network connectivity and reduce passenger volumes on profitable connecting routes
Airport contractual obligations may slow or prevent exit from unprofitable routes
next_steps: Research competitors' cost basis on Pacific NW routes and identify specific operational levers (scheduling, turnaround time, crew utilization) to begin matching their cost structure
Consider cross-training employees to reduce the volume of layoffs required in Marketing and IT
Identify and execute a detailed plan to reduce Marketing and IT costs by ~25%, including vendor consolidation, outsourcing evaluation, and headcount optimization
Evaluate route demand trends before making any final decisions on cutting the Portland-Seattle or Denver-Portland routes
